teaser: The Eiffel Tower, painted as if it were exploding and dancing at the same time.
review_notes:
The Art Institute of Chicago dates the work 1911/23 (begun 1911, reworked by Delaunay in 1923); the catalog year is 1911.
Size about 160.7 x 128.6 cm.
Tower facts: completed 1889, about 300 m, tallest structure in the world until 1930, permit for 20 years, kept in part thanks to its use as a radio antenna: verify wording.
Original 1889 paint described as reddish brown: verify.
Delaunay in the first Blaue Reiter exhibition, Munich, December 1911; Klee visiting him in Paris in 1912.
Apollinaire coining 'Orphism' in 1912.
The rounded yellow and white forms are read as clouds or puffs of light: interpretation.
Number of tower paintings in the series given loosely as 'around ten' between 1909 and 1912.

lesson.text: How would you paint something 300 meters (about 1,000 ft) tall if you were standing almost at its feet? Tilt your head back and the top slides away. Look down and the legs spread out of view. No single glance holds it. In 1911 that was Robert Delaunay's problem, and this canvas is what he did about it.

He was 26. The tower was 22, younger than he was. It had gone up in 1889 as the entrance arch of a world's fair, a naked iron frame with no stone on it, and for two decades many Parisians had called it an eyesore. Delaunay loved it without irony. He painted it around ten times between 1909 and 1912.

The tower was supposed to come down. Its permit ran for only twenty years. Gustave Eiffel saved it by making it useful to science, above all as a giant antenna for the new wireless telegraph. By the time Delaunay set up his easel, it was beaming radio signals across France.

His solution to the too-tall problem was simple and radical: stop choosing. Paint the view looking up, the view looking down and the view straight ahead, and bolt them onto one tower. Travel up it from the ground and watch the viewpoint change under you.

lesson.title: Up the tower
lesson.text: Three levels, three different angles of view.

spots.title: The legs
spots.text: They splay outward like a person bracing on a rocking boat. You see the iron lattice from below and from the side at once, with a great arch opening between the feet.

spots.title: The first platform
spots.text: Here you are suddenly looking down onto the deck, as if hovering in front of it. The floor tips toward you like a tray about to spill.

spots.title: The summit
spots.text: The top does not end in a point. It breaks into loose girders and melts into white and yellow light, the way a very tall thing fades when you crane your neck at it.

lesson.text: Legs from underneath, platform from above, summit lost in glare. Stacked together, the views make the tower buckle at the waist. It is not falling. It is what your neck and eyes go through in the five seconds it takes to look it up and down.
Delaunay paints the experience of looking instead of the object. The broken tower is a record of an eye in motion.

This is a Cubist idea, and Delaunay had learned it from Picasso and Braque. But their pictures of these years were small, brown and gray, and about bottles and guitars. His is over 1.6 meters high (more than 5 ft), blazing red, and about the most modern structure on earth. He wanted Cubism out of the studio and into the street.

The red is less far-fetched than it looks. When the tower opened in 1889 its ironwork wore a reddish-brown coat of paint. It has been repainted many times since, in shades from yellow-ochre to today's bronze-brown, and each repainting takes tons of paint.
Now pull back from the tower to the edges of the canvas. Something frames it left and right, and that frame is doing half the work of making the tower look alive.
How the picture is staged, like a theater.

lines.label: Left curtain
lines.text: A stack of dark apartment buildings, brown and black, bowing inward. They are old stone Paris, heavy and shadowed.

lines.label: Right curtain
lines.text: Blue-gray buildings bend the opposite way. Together the two sides part like drapes, and the tower appears in the bright gap between them.

lines.label: The spine
lines.text: The tower's axis is no straight line. It leans, kinks at the platform and kicks left at the base. Against the stiff walls, the iron seems to sway.

lesson.text: Dark, old and stony on the sides. Bright, new and iron in the middle. The contrast is the message. Delaunay is not documenting a monument. He is cheering for a century that has only just started, with its engineers, its airplanes and its radio waves.
The sky joins in. Around the upper half of the tower float rounded shapes that are neither quite cloud nor quite sun. They are the first hint of where Delaunay's painting was heading next.
Find the cluster of soft, round, yellow-and-white puffs beside the tower.

spots.title: Clouds, or light itself
spots.text: Curved, creamy forms with yellow hearts, set against sharp green and white wedges. They are the only round things in a picture made of angles. Within a year Delaunay would paint circles of color and nothing else.

lesson.text: Those circles became a style of their own. In 1912 the poet Guillaume Apollinaire called it Orphism, after Orpheus, the musician of Greek myth, because the colors were meant to work on you directly, as notes do. The tower was the last recognizable thing Delaunay painted before he let subject matter go.

The tower pictures made Delaunay more famous in Germany than at home. In December 1911 he was invited to show in Munich with the Blue Rider group led by Wassily Kandinsky and Franz Marc. The young Paul Klee traveled to Paris the next year to meet him.
One last tour of the surface, at your own pace. Much of the fun is in how quickly the paint moves between the solid and the dissolved.

spots.title: The white block
spots.text: A pale apartment house, its windows reduced to black dashes, leaning as if blown by the same wind as the tower. It crowds right up against the tower's feet.

spots.title: The arcade
spots.text: A row of tiny arches rings the first platform. The real gallery had them too. Delaunay keeps this one accurate detail so you never doubt which building this is.

spots.title: Old Paris
spots.text: Cornices, balconies and shutters in brown and black, piled up the left edge. Painted thickly and darkly, as if seen from inside a narrow street.

spots.title: Splinters of sky
spots.text: White, turquoise and green shards. The air around the tower is as fractured as the tower. For Delaunay light was a substance, something that could break things.

spots.title: The orange arch
spots.text: One of the huge arches between the legs, painted in thin orange with a pale house showing through. Iron has become almost transparent.

spots.title: Crossed girders
spots.text: The X-shaped braces of the shaft, in dark and bright red. Each face of the tower gets its own shade, so the column seems to twist as it rises.

lesson.text: Stand under the real tower some day and tip your head back until you nearly lose your balance. That lurch in the stomach is the true subject here. Delaunay did come back to this canvas years later to rework it, as though the question at its start, how to paint what will not fit in one look, never quite stopped nagging him.

quiz.question: Why does the tower look broken in the middle?
options: Delaunay combined views from several angles
It shows the tower during construction
The canvas was damaged and repaired
quiz.explanation: He joined the views looking up, down and straight ahead into one tower.

quiz.question: What saved the real Eiffel Tower from being taken down?
options: Its use as a radio antenna
quiz.explanation: Eiffel made it useful to science, above all for wireless telegraphy.

quiz.question: What frames the tower on both sides of the canvas?
quiz.explanation: Old stone buildings bend apart like drapes around the bright tower.

quiz.question: Who invented the name “Orphism” for Delaunay's art of pure color?
quiz.explanation: The poet Apollinaire coined it in 1912, after the musician Orpheus.

quiz.question: How did Delaunay's tower differ from Picasso's and Braque's Cubist pictures of the time?
options: It was large, colorful and about a modern subject
quiz.explanation: Their works were small, muted still lifes; his is big, red and urban.

quiz.question: Which accurate detail keeps the building recognizable?
options: The row of small arches on the first platform
quiz.explanation: The arcade around the first level is rendered faithfully.

facts.text: When Delaunay painted it, the Eiffel Tower was younger than he was.
facts.explanation: The tower dated from 1889 and was 22; Delaunay was 26.

facts.text: Delaunay painted the Eiffel Tower only once.
facts.explanation: He painted it around ten times between 1909 and 1912.

facts.text: The tower pictures were ignored in Germany.
facts.explanation: They got him invited to exhibit with the Blue Rider group in Munich in 1911.
